en: Preface to the Essential Exegesis Following the Text of the Commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuanjue xuduoliao yi jing*).
This *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, which clarifies the definitive meaning, is the manifest manual for realizing the nature and the essential guide to the One Vehicle.

Its expounded principles are profound and mysterious, beyond the reach of words or images; its textual meanings are hidden and arcane, transcending the conceptual deliberations of those of the Two Vehicles.
How great is the nature of enlightenment! It perfectly encompasses the ten directions; cause and effect are fused, and the true and the false interpenetrate.
Yet sentient beings remain unaware and ignorant, stumbling in delusion upon the path of health and suffering the pains of poverty.

Even those who resolve to seek it with joy are distracted by the four afflictions and dazed by the three contemplations. Consequently, they are unable to realize perfect enlightenment as it truly is—save for the Tathāgata alone.
Having fully attained its great function, it seizes the opportune moment to initiate its destiny, appearing for the benefit of the world.
Although the four minds are observed as equal, because the three faculties differ, the distinctions between sudden and gradual awakening and cultivation arise.

This sutra is like the Tathāgata entering the Land of Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*), manifesting the Body of Enjoyment (*sambhoga-kāya*), and suddenly revealing the truth to Mañjuśrī, Vajragarbha, and other great bodhisattvas who have ascended to reality.
This work explains the Dharma-practice of the Ground of Coming and the Source of the Pure Awakening-Mind of Sentient Beings;
its teaching and listening accord in profound harmony, and it exhaustively investigates principle and phenomena to provide true knowledge of the Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning.

Master Dinghui of Guifeng received the Heart-Seal of the Southern School and was among those who personally heard [the teachings] from Qingliang. Whenever he contemplated this scripture, he regarded it as the dwelling place for his spirit, and thus he composed a commentary upon it.
His commentaries, numbering tens of thousands of words, proceed with both breadth and concision; his vision of the Dharma is clear, and his profound mind is uniquely awakened.

His exposition of principles is perfect, and his spirit is transcendent and peerless. With great vigor, he widely proclaimed the teachings and brought forth the true essence. Consequently, his fame overflowed throughout the Nine Provinces and his reputation soared across the Four Seas.
Those who carried their book-cases in competition to follow him and those who came from afar clutching their lead pencils were like water flowing downward. Alas!

How magnificent and ultimate! It is beyond words to praise. In the Song dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Qingyuan, who followed the teachings of Guifeng and exerted himself in commenting upon and sub-commenting [the scriptures].

He established the orthodoxy and heterodoxy of various masters, distinguished the right and wrong of the hundred schools, searched out the doctrines of the extensive sections of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and attained profound realization of the essential tenets of Xianshou and Qingliang.
He then praised and propagated the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*). As for its immediate application...
A compendium was compiled in twelve fascicles, titled *Suíwén yàojiě* (Essential Explanations Following the Text). Its meaning is abundant while its phrasing is concise;
it raises the most essential points without omission and explains the most subtle points with complete thoroughness.

Truly, as for that which illuminates the black pearl of the vast ocean and brightens the cassia orb of the azure sky—it is none other than the *Suíwén yàojiě*. As for this book, the *Yàojiě*, it had not yet been circulated.
I, Shi Yu, have fortunately possessed this work in my private collection for many years.

Recently, the Śrī Saṃgharakṣita of Longbao Monastery came to request that I publish it in woodblocks so as to broaden its dissemination among those in the world who have cursorily studied the *Awakening of Faith*.
Praising his aspiration, I granted my consent and added annotations and punctuation to accompany it, hoping that students may reach a thorough understanding through these essential explanations.
Preface: Because this commentary uses its exegesis to penetrate the sūtra and directly accord with the Buddha’s intent, I have composed this preface.

Written on the Buddha’s birthday in the fourth month of the year Etsuin (the eleventh year of the Genroku era, the Wood-Tiger year), by the śramaṇa Śrāvastī, Dōsho, Head Official of the Kegon School at Tōdai-ji, beneath Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Essential Explanations Following the Text of the Commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Including Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Qingyuan.

Regarding the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, a scripture of definitive meaning: it is the Tathāgata, having entered the land of quiescent light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), manifesting his body of enjoyment (*sambhogakāya*).

For the sake of those great beings who have ascended to the truth, those of superior faculties among ordinary people, and those with the capacity for the One Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching, he preached in accordance with their nature, employing metaphors such as the open space, the great white ox-cart, the non-existent city, and the removal of filth.
While these teachings are difficult to categorize within the five periods of the Buddha's life, they are fully subsumed within the Perfect and Sudden.
Were it not for the elucidation of great beings, who could have accorded with the fundamental purport of this sutra? Thus spoke the Bodhisattva of the Great Tang.

The Commentary on the Treatise by Chan Master Dinghui of Guifeng: This sutra has been widely propagated through ancient and modern times, its influence pure and far-reaching. Due to the planting of roots in past lives, I have had the fortune to encounter this scripture.
Having no fixed teacher, I attended various renowned seats of learning, where I devoted myself to inquiry and questioning, contemplating with deep thought and refining my understanding.

Although I have barely managed to avoid the loss of the sheep [the path], I have ultimately not escaped the counting of treasures [the attachment to phenomena]. Having ascended to the stage of initial reception, I entered the gate of Yuanquan.
(The Master’s name was Rubao. He thus realized the principle of "throwing a mustard seed into a needle's eye," fully awakening to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.

Whether in moments of distress or in ordinary daily activities, he practiced this realization moment by moment, remaining in constant resonance with it. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he enjoyed its vibrant, lively functioning without end.

Having been honored as the Second Seat at the Master’s dharma-seat, he surpassed others; though previously hindered by intellectual explanations, he was ultimately nurtured and transformed by the Master.

Having recently accepted the command to reside in Piling and assumed the humble office of abbot at Huayan, amidst the intervals between sweeping and sprinkling, I have expounded these teachings for my disciples.

Allowing myself to retire from the assembly, I await the end of my days among the forests and springs, accompanied by two or three fellow monks who follow me to cultivate the Way through meditation and recitation.

Beyond these practices, I have further elucidated this text; thus, I have extracted the essentials according to the passages and directly resolved doubts and difficulties, providing scholars with a thorough basis for investigation.

I have composed this commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, titled the *Essential Exegesis Following the Text of the Commentary and Sub-commentary*, which extends to over one hundred and ninety thousand words in twelve fascicles.
How could I dare claim to be worthy of those who have attained mastery? It is merely intended for those at the beginning stage of their practice.
Should there be anything that does not accord with the truth, it is difficult to reach a definitive judgment; I hope that future students will correct me. Nevertheless, even a speck of dust...
Nurtured by Mount Hua and Mount Yue, yet the droplets fall into the vast ocean; my efforts are in vain, resulting only in exhaustion. I know not how to increase its height or broaden its expanse;
let it be that others blame me—this is surely my lot.

Written on the day of the full moon, when the handle of the Dipper points toward the constellation Chunchu, in the year of Guiyou, the sixth year of the Jiading era of the Great Song. Preface respectfully composed.
Essential Explanations Following the Text of the Commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Qingyuan.

The "Outline of the General Title" refers to the general title of the commentary on the sutra. The title is given as *Lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary); whereas the *Dashu* (Great Commentary) provides annotated explanations of the sutra.
The essential meaning of this work is directly applied to the root scripture, and it is titled *Lüshù Zhùjīng* (A Brief Commentary and Annotation of the Scripture).

This is similar to Changshui’s commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which is also called *Yìshù Zhùjīng* (An Exegesis of Meaning and Annotation of the Scripture). The section headings state that the titles of such "scripture-commentary" works share this same significance.

Thus, by using the commentary to annotate the scripture, the scripture becomes the primary subject while the commentary is secondary; since the host and guest are thus distinguished, both are employed together as the title.

Regarding the titles of the sutra commentaries (*jing shu*): if one refers to a commentary that is circulated separately from the text, it is called the "title of the commentary" (*shu ti*), not the general title of the sutra commentary.

Furthermore, there are two types of titles: those placed at the head of the sutra are called "sutra titles" (*jing ti*), while those appearing before the commentary are called "commentary headings" (*shu mu*).

To speak specifically of this Great Commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuanjue jing da shu*), "Complete Enlightenment" is the name of the sutra being explained, while the "Great Commentary" is the name of the commentary itself.

This refers to the commentaries (*śāstra*) that can explain [the sūtras]; it means selecting and extracting the titles of the sūtras that are to be explained, as seen in works such as the *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra* (*Hṛdaya-sūtra-ṭīkā*).

One should understand other cases by analogy. Some say that the phrase "marking the general title" refers to the general title of a single commentary in contrast to the specific chapters of meaning (*arthapada*) that follow;
others say it refers to the specific explanation of the sūtra’s title that follows. However, this serves to adorn the holy teachings (*ārya-śāsana*).

Regarding the statement, "There is nothing that cannot be asked," the *Commentary on the Practice and Vows* (*Xingyuan Shu*) asks: "How does this differ from the 'Explanation of the General Title' (*Shi zongti*)?
The answer is: That [previous section] opens into two sections: first, the title of the sūtra being explained, and second, the title of the commentary explaining it.

Within the section explaining the title of the sūtra, it says "Explanation of the General Title" (*Shi zongti*), which is in contrast to what follows, namely the specific explanation of the chapter titles. It is within the subsequent section, the actual explanation of the sūtra's title itself, that the term "General Title" (*zongti*) is used.
The Commentary states: "This is the general title for the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*, and it does not overlap with the title of this brief commentary, which is also called a *sūtra*.

Question: Master Jin-yun’s record of the Heart Sūtra names it the *Xianzheng* (Exposing the Correct), referring to it as the general title, while the *Lianzhu* (String of Pearls) refers to it as the title of the commentary (*shu*).
Some say that the *Lianzhu* implicitly critiques the *Xianzheng*, while others say this is not the case; I do not know which is correct.

Regarding the inquiry into the ultimate purpose: the answer is that there is no difference between an independent treatise (*kant-xing*) and a commentary on a sūtra (*chu-jing*); why then should one criticize it?
Since he has already moved the preface from the commentary on the sūtra to serve as the general title for the "Sūtra-Commentary" (*jing-shu*), there is no error in principle.

For instance, when Changshui moved the preface in his *Vajra-sūtra Commentary*, he likewise titled it a "Sūtra-Commentary. Similarly, when Guifeng moved the preface in his *Awakening of Faith Commentary*, he also titled it a "Treatise-Commentary" (*lun-shu*).
If it is argued that this demonstrates that Guifeng was incorrect, how could that be so? Question:

Are the titles of the *Qǐxìn lüèshū zhùjīng* (Brief Commentary on the Awakening of Faith with Annotations on the Sutra) and the *Huáyán xīnjīng shūsù kàngxíng shùtí* (Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Avatamsaka, with Notes on the Obstructed Practice and Title) the same as those of the current *Lüèshū zhùjīng*? Answer: Although the old titles remain, their meaning is no different.

For instance, beneath the title of the *Qǐxìn*, there is a marginal note stating: "Moved by [Master] Mou, the commentary was annotated for the treatise. Thus, the Jinshui [Master Huaigan]... [text ends].

Yan’s relocation of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) to the sūtra follows the same principle (one should say that while the general title was moved, he instead moved the title of the sub-commentary; the fact that Qingliang’s ancient outline appears reversed is merely a result of misplaced collation).

Understand this by analogy with cases where the *Xin jing* (Heart Sūtra) sub-commentaries were not altered from their original titles. If one does not add marginal notes, there will inevitably be minor flaws;
thus, for a concise commentary on the sūtra, I have taken the essential points from the extensive commentaries and annotated them directly onto the sūtra text.

"Below," it says, "is 'er' (a suffix). Regarding the term *shū* (commentary): it means "sparse" (*sō*) and "to resolve" (*ketsu*). It refers to sparsely [explaining] the scriptural text and resolving its underlying meaning.

Regarding the term *chū* (annotation): it is derived either from the radical for speech or from the radical for water. If derived from speech, it signifies "instruction" (*kun*) or "explanation" (*ge*).

To instruct and explain is to cause the textual relations to become manifest. If derived from water, it signifies "to resolve" (*ketsu*) or "to flow" (*ryū*). It is like resolving and flowing [water] so that there is no obstruction.

The phrase "the appearance of a stream flowing without ceasing" refers to the five characters of the *Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra* (Dafangguang yuanjue), which are the sūtra being commented upon;

what follows below consists of the commentary (*śāstra*) capable of commenting upon it, Volume One. This represents the sequence of the scroll. Generally, there are five schools of commentary on this sūtra:
first, the one-volume commentary by Dharma Master Weiqu of Baoguo Temple in the Capital; second, the [commentary] by Wuxiang of Xiantian Temple...
1. Master Shi’s Commentary in two fascicles; 2. Master Daoquan of Haizang Monastery in the Northern Capital’s Commentary in three fascicles;
3. Master Jianzhi of Jianfu Monastery in the Great Tang’s Commentary in four fascicles; 4.

Master Guifeng Dinghui’s Extensive Commentary in three fascicles, its Sub-commentary (*Cao*) in thirteen fascicles, its Abridged Commentary in two fascicles, and its Abridged Sub-commentary in six fascicles; 5. *The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization at the Dharma Site*.

The various commentaries on the preceding eighteen fascicles were either overly prolix or too concise; they had not been pruned, and thus they deviated from the core tenets of the Sūtra, remaining untransmitted in the world.

Guifeng’s work, however, is followed by both the ancients and the moderns; it circulates throughout the four seas and remains unobstructed to this day. The term "zhù" (commentary) includes the preface and the "cong" (concordance);

"he" (integration) means that the *Jiyùn* dictionary records it as an entering tone, signifying both "together" and "inclusive. Since there is additionally a preface outside the main commentary, [it is so designated].
The Cloud [Commentary], together with its Preface: In order to follow the principle of brevity, I have not established a separate title for the preface;

rather, it is appended beneath the title of the sub-commentary (*śū*), so that the title of the sub-commentary serves simultaneously as the title of the preface. Now, "preface" (*xu*) means "to narrate"; it refers to the narration of the great purport of this single scripture as well as the causes and conditions for the composition of the sub-commentary.
Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) also means "school" (*xiangxu*); as the *Erya* states, it refers to the eastern and western walls [of a school].
It is said: "To know the depth of a residence, one first observes the school; to know a person, one first observes the forehead and eyes;
to know the intention of a composer, one first observes the preface. Mount Zhongnan is the southernmost extremity of Chang'an;
it is named Zhongnan and also called Taiyi Mountain. It corresponds above to the Taiyi star and is so named because it is the dwelling place of that star.
Since ancient times, many renowned monks have resided on this mountain. The Caotang Temple is a branch monastery of Zhongnan Mountain. As for the term "si" (temple):
when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, they stayed at the Honglu Temple; later, they moved elsewhere, and monasteries such as Baima were separately established.
To this day, the quarters of the monks are called "si. The term "shamen" (śramaṇa) is the general designation for those of the Śākya clan.
It is also rendered as *śramaṇa*, which here means "one who lacks the Way. This refers to one who eliminates the lack [of virtue] by cultivating the Right Path.
It is also called "diligent rest," meaning to diligently refine the three karmas and to cease all delusive thoughts. Furthermore, the Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:

"To leave home and abandon kin, to realize the mind and reach the fundamental source, and to understand the dharma of non-action—this is called a śramaṇa. Now, there are four types of śramaṇas: first, [the renunciant śramaṇa]... (text continues).
1. The defiled-path śramaṇa; 2. the śramaṇa who speaks of the path; 3. the śramaṇa who lives by the path; and 4. the ultimate (paramārtha) śramaṇa.

Regarding these, the commentator [Yuan Ce] states that among the latter two—the śramaṇa who speaks of the path and the śramaṇa who lives by the path—if one considers their original nature, they are great powers manifesting in the world, and thus they are ultimate śramaṇas.
However, in the Western Regions (India), there are non-Buddhist śramaṇas; therefore, the word "Śākya" is sometimes prefixed to distinguish them from these. This...
Since there is no fixed rule regarding this, it need not necessarily be added. As for the *Nanshan lüchao*, it also retains the character "shì" (釋);

its retention does not hinder [the identification]. Zongmi is the name of the commentator (*shuzhu*); his surname was He, and he was a native of Xichong County in Guozhou. Having abandoned Confucianism to follow the Buddhist path, his brilliant insight was peerless.
He encountered the teachings of the Southern School of Chan and encountered this scripture [of the Huayan school]. His commentary on the *Huayan jing* was seen at the capital.
The Master, State Preceptor Qingliang, said: "Viluzanghai, you who can follow me on my travels—will it be you? Thereafter, he took no fixed teacher;
he surveyed all the various schools, upheld the Vinaya, and elucidated the *Vijñaptimātratā*. Among those who contended for the four kingdoms [of Buddhist doctrine], none could surpass him.

In the second year of the Dàhé era, during the Qíngchéng Festival, he was summoned [the character "zhēng" is used here as a verb meaning "to summon," as it coincides with the temple name of Emperor Rénzōng].

He was summoned during the reign of Emperor Wenzong (the Great Harmony), where he entered the inner palace to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma and was granted a purple robe and square-cut cassock. He subsequently requested to return to the mountains.
On the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Huichang era, he passed away while seated at the Xingfu Pagoda Cloister.

His body was cremated, yielding several thousand grains of śarīra, which were brilliant white, lustrous, and large. Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dinghui; he was the foremost successor of the Huayan school.
The Seven Patriarchs are also included; their other writings and deeds are fully recorded in the biography of the Minister Pei (Pei Xiu). Regarding the authorship of this commentary:

that which is composed by a sage is called a "sage-work" (*shu*), while that which is compiled by others is called "clarified" (*ming*). To say "I transmit" (*shu*) rather than "I compose" (*zuo*) reflects the humility of the commentator.

As the *Book of Rites* states: "Confucius took Yao and Shun as his ancestral legacy and followed the statutes of Wen and Wu; above, he regulated the heavenly patterns, and below, he conformed to the ways of earth and water."
It is just as Zhongni said: "I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity, and I venture to compare myself to my elder brother La Peng.

This preface demonstrates the essence of the awakened mind and the characteristics of the awakening of the mind. Indeed, this introduction constitutes the pivotal core of the entire scripture. It is divided into three parts:
revealing the principle, clarifying the teaching, and providing the commentary. First, regarding the revelation of the principle, it is further divided into two sections concerning the mind.

The character "also" (*ye*) below immediately indicates the essence of the awakened mind (*jue zhi xintti*): that all phenomena are false and illusory, transcending the realm of thought and deliberation.
This immediately indicates the aspect of the mind’s awakening (*xin zhi juexiang*). The essence of the awakened mind is like a perfectly luminous pearl;

it is the essence that manifests through its aspect. The aspect of the mind’s awakening is like the luster of the pearl; it is the aspect that manifests from its essence. Thus, regarding the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]—
Although the essence and characteristics of the teaching are fused, they constitute different gates and must not be confused or merged as one.

As the subsequent text explains the "ground of the mind of original enlightenment" (*benjue xindi*): "Original enlightenment" refers to the awakened aspect of the mind, while the "ground of the mind" refers to the essential substance of that awakening.
From this, one knows that these two sections are distinct, as it says: "Neither going nor coming," and so forth, up to "the solitary moon in the cassia tree."
Its brightness in the azure sky is the very substance of the mind, which is neither born nor extinguished;
its pervasive purity and even its ultimate identity with all things are the virtuous functions of the mind-substance itself.

This is because all phenomena are none other than the virtuous characteristics and functional activities within the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), just as vessels are made of gold or clarity is the nature of a mirror. However, gold...
No vessel other than the Perfect and Sudden Teaching can accommodate this;
therefore, while these two categories are spoken of as fused and identical, they must not be treated as the same when discussed as distinct gates, nor should they be confused or conflated.
[The commentary states: "Great, penetrating, advantageous, and correct are the virtues of Qian;

beginning with the single breath (one qi), eternal joy, selfhood, purity, and clarity are the virtues of the Buddha, rooted in the one mind. This refers to the source of the mind by way of the resultant virtues.
These resultant virtues are the four virtues of the Buddha, while the source of the mind is the fundamental source of all defiled and pure phenomena. First, one must investigate this one mind.
That which serves as the foundation for the virtues of the fruit is so because it corresponds to the "One Qi" (One Vital Energy) of Confucianism being the foundation for the virtue of Qian;
however, this is stated merely in terms of opposition, hence it says that "the One Mind is the foundation of the Four Virtues.
If one were to speak according to the ultimate reality, this One Mind is the fundamental source of all dharmas; the original intention is to clarify the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment.

The mind is the foundation of all virtues; thus, [the author] first cites an analogy, stating that "Original, Auspicious, Beneficial, and Correct" (*yuan-heng-li-zhen*) are the virtues of *Qian* (Heaven).

Since these originate from the single breath (*yiqi*), one knows that this merely cites an analogy. From this, the general category is termed "summarizing through resultant virtue" (*yue guode*), which aims to point toward the source of the mind.
Because the single breath of Confucianism is regarded as the root of yin-yang and heaven-and-earth, this analogy is applied to Buddhism.
The teaching holds that the single mind is the root of all dharmas. Regarding the "Preface to the *Lüchāo*," there is a separate preface outside the main text;
thus, it is called the "Preface to the *Chāo*. It was not composed by the author of the *Chāo* himself, which is why it is separately titled:
"Preface to the *Lüchāo* of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment. Liu Xi of Wumen (Wu refers to Wu-Yu) said: "Taibo yielded and did not accept [the throne], returning [to the mountains]."
He established his fief here to satisfy his aspirations. Sima Qian, in his "Genealogy of Taibo," states that when Jin destroyed the state of Yu in China, it was because Su was considered Central Wu.
Fan Ning remarked: "Taibo" is a title signifying "Great Goodness.
He was the eldest son of King Tai of Zhou; thus he was called Taibo. Because Zhongyong and the younger Ji Li were both virtuous, [Taibo departed].

The virtue of Taibo’s renunciation was profound and far-reaching; even a sage could not surpass it. As for the *Sishan* (Teacher of Zhi), he was a contemporary of the Dharma Master Jin-yun, though his specific deeds and conduct remain undetailed.
The preface sometimes divides [the chapters] into five or seven sections; here, they are divided into eleven.
The first section clarifies what is received:
[as for the cultivation of the body, it is nothing other than the precepts; as for the harmonizing of the mind, it is nothing other than Perfect Enlightenment].
This inquiry into the cultivation of the body serves as the introduction that gives rise to the subsequent text, meaning:
To practice the myriad deeds as the way of cultivating the person is solely through the precepts;

to clearly investigate the enlightened nature and dissolve the deluded consciousness is solely through Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). That one first observes the precepts and subsequently integrates the mind speaks of the gradual progression by which the Way is received.
"Second, a general account of those who received [the transmission] (and as for the word 'and' [in the phrase 'both... and...'], it means 'together,' 'simultaneously,' and 'privilege';
'vowei' means 'humble' or 'lowly'; the commentary on the *Hanshu* states it means 'accumulated,' implying that one has been fortunate enough to receive both together)."

I received this from the gate of Great Master Jinghui. His name was Shanzheng; his deeds and activities are not detailed. Third, I shall separately clarify where [the teachings] lead back [to their source].

For the time being, I shall follow what I have heard and engage in the practice, while concurrently lecturing on the *Zhigui* (Pointing to the Goal). In my later years, I took the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-citta* (Perfect Enlightenment) as my essential focus.
The *Shuo* says: "The gentleman is filial when at home and deferential when abroad; he is careful and trustworthy, loves the multitude broadly, and draws near to the benevolent.
When his conduct has surplus energy, he uses it to study the cultural arts. The *Jingyi* explains:

"Being filial at home and deferential abroad, acting with care and speaking with sincerity, dwelling among the multitude with broad love, and choosing friends to draw near to the benevolent—this is the fundamental duty of the gentleman."
If there is something one is unable to do, one should strive to do it; if there is something one has not yet attained, one should exert effort to reach it.
Only when these have become sufficient does one then engage in the cultivation of literary expression. Thus, in that case, engaging in such practice is the study of literature;
in this case, one merely practices at intervals what one has heard of the Way, while also engaging in public lectures. Therefore, it is said that "engaging in practice" encompasses both.
I have lectured on and practiced the precepts while cultivating the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*), concurrently engaging in chanting;

I have also devoted myself to the Vinaya while lecturing on this scripture. However, regarding these two paths, those who set out on their journey at evening and place them side by side find that they take the *Complete Enlightenment* as the essential and subtle teaching.
The fourth chapter’s commentary is comprehensive and vast;

its author, [his] grandfather, Yan the Commentator—namely, the Chan Master Dinghui of Guifeng—composed the *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary) in two fascicles and the *Lüechao* (Brief Sub-commentary) in six fascicles.

The commentary serves to penetrate the sutras, while the sub-commentary serves to penetrate the commentary; it explores the profound and seeks out the hidden, with concise phrasing yet expansive meaning. Thus...
[Preface by Prime Minister Pei] The *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) say: "To explore the mysterious, seek out the hidden, hook the profound, and reach the distant.

Here, "explore" (*tan*) means to investigate; "mysterious" (*ze*) refers to the abstruse; "seek" (*suo*) means to pursue; and "hidden" (*yin*) refers to the subtle and obscure. Thus, the commentaries and sub-commentaries of Guifeng are those that investigate, seek, and pursue the profound, the abstruse, the dark, and the subtle.
Yet their phrasing is concise and appropriate, while their principles are comprehensive and vast, encompassing the five thousand words [of the *Daodejing*].
The essential purport of the *Zhongxuan* (The Pivot) is fully contained in the preface by Lord Pei.

Regarding the *Wubie tantiyao chao* (Excerpts on the Five Distinct Sighs), Master Daogu was its lineage holder down to the present day; among those who drive the chariot of the teachings today, there are none who do not take this commentary as their standard.
[Regarding the compass: The Way is inherently based on teachers; thus, when one has a teacher, the Way can be honored, and when one has a standard for speech, affairs can be modeled upon.
Now that our Patriarch Guifeng has a clear lineage of transmission, his commentaries and sub-commentaries have spread their fragrance through past and present without fading.
His words surpass those of mere exegesis. Yangzi said: "Is the Way not found in Zhongni? Zhongni surpassed all in his exegesis.
"Is it not found here among the Confucians? The commentary states: "Jia (駕) means to transmit; 'zi' (茲) refers to the *si-nan* (司南). 'Si' (司) means to preside over;

[Aspiring to emulate those who are clear-sighted, I, though dull-witted, am fortunate to have this teaching spread before me. I constantly fear that the sacred words may become confused like water and cranes, and I deeply worry that those who transmit them may err as if mistaking "lu" for "yu.
*Meng* (pronounced *móu kǒng*) and *mèi*: "Meng" means disordered or bewildered; it refers to being lost. "Mèi" means dark or obscure. I refer to myself thus.

I am utterly ignorant and dim-witted; it is my great good fortune to have been granted the opportunity to expound this teaching. Yet, regarding the words of the Sage, I am ever filled with anxiety and trepidation.

I deeply fear errors such as confusing "water" (shui) for "crane" (he), or the transmission of "ox" (lu) for "fish" (yu). Regarding the confusion between "water" (shui) and "crane" (he): some editions read "dried up" (kuhe) instead of "crane" (she).
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states that Ānanda went to a bamboo grove and heard two bhikṣus reciting a verse.

Ānanda said: "This is not the Buddha’s word; you should listen as I recite [the true teaching]:

The seventh section generally describes the collation and verification [of various editions through consultation with Master Zhongxi of Wulin, comparing numerous versions against canonical texts, following the principle of honoring the ancient and disparaging the modern,

Jinshui Zeng studied under him and produced the six-fascicle *Lengyan jing jinheng chao*, the one-fascicle *Xinjing xianzheng ji*, and the four-fascicle *Kangyō raihan gisho kanketsu*, all of which circulate in the world today.
When I consulted him regarding the principles of literary composition, he [responded] as follows.
I have searched through various scriptures and do not dare to act with superficiality; "following" means to follow the venerable ancients.

Where there are doubts or discrepancies in their explanations, I likewise do not dare to arbitrarily engage in emendation, adhering instead to the principle that the historian leaves blank spaces for missing texts. As the *Lunyu* records:
The Master said, "I am still able to recall when the scribes left blanks for missing characters. Even if one had horses, he would lend them to others to ride."

"Alas, they have now perished! The *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) commentary states: "The 'Shi' (Historian) was the official in charge of writing; those who held the brush at his side were made to record events.

'Wen' (Text/Script) refers to characters. When the excellent historians of antiquity encountered doubts regarding characters in their records, they would leave them blank to await those more capable, never daring to engage in forced interpretation.
Confucius said, 'I am still able to see these ancient historians leaving blanks where there was doubt.'"
This passage uses an analogy to illustrate that one who possesses a horse but cannot train it well should borrow someone else’s to ride and practice with. "Wang" (亡) means "to lack.
When he saw that people were acting in such a deficient manner, he expressed his doubt; even until now, such [corruptions] do not exist [in the original].

Therefore, Zhongni also left it blank and did not record it in the *Chunqiu*, for the *Chunqiu* is the historical record of the state of Lu;
yet even the modern commentators have ventured to touch upon this point, and though there are some grounds for doubt, they too do not dare to alter it arbitrarily.

Preface dated the full moon of the month of the Bird’s Beak (Chūnzhòu) in the year of Xinsi, the second year of the Kangding era of the Great Song Dynasty.
"Great Song" signifies its imperial majesty. "Song" was formerly Shangqiu; it was the city of Suiyang in Liang Commandery during the Han dynasty, which is present-day Nanjing.
When King Wu of Zhou defeated Zhou, he enfeoffed the descendants of Yin; Micizi received this fief and established it as the state of Song.

Because the Great Ancestor Emperor (Emperor Taizu) had been enfeoffed by the Zhou as the Duke of Song, and subsequently ascended the throne as the九五 (the Nine-Five, i.e., the Son of Heaven), he took his former fief as the name for his reign over all under heaven.
He subsequently made Dongjing his capital. The period of Kangding refers to the era of our present dynasty’s Renzong.

The "ladle" (*biǎo*) refers to the handle of the dipper, which is the seventh star of the Northern Dipper (*Beidǒu*). The handle of the dipper revolves in accordance with the four seasons, each pointing toward a different direction.

In summer, it points south; furthermore, it is divided into three positions: in the fourth month it points to *Chūn-wěi* (the Tail of the Quail), in the fifth month to *Chūn-huǒ* (the Fire of the Quail), and in the sixth month to *Chūn-shǒu* (the Head of the Quail), also called *Chūn-zhòu*.
*Zhòu* (pronounced *zhù jiù*) is the same as *huì* (the beak). In this month, the handle of the dipper points toward...

"The *Chūnshǒu* (Bird’s Head) corresponds to the fifth month in the Xia calendar and the sixth month in the Shang; the *Chúnhuǒ* (Fire of the Bird) corresponds to the sixth month in the Xia calendar and the seventh month in the Shang;

the *Chūnwěi* (Tail of the Bird) corresponds to the seventh month in the Xia calendar and the eighth month in the Shang. The fifteenth day is the time of the full moon, because the sun and moon are positioned opposite one another.
Therefore, the sixteenth day is called "already at the full moon" (*jìwàng*); *jì* means "already," signifying that it has already passed the point of the full moon.

[Guifeng] refers to a specific peak of Mount Zhongnan; because the shape and configuration of this peak resemble a jade scepter (*gui*), it was named accordingly.

The full term is *āraṇya*, also called *āraṇyaka*; this means a "place of tranquility," referring to a monastic dwelling.
This is the general designation [for the classics].
[The various canons reach their pinnacle in the Book of Changes (Zhouyi). The origins of the Changes began with Fuxi, who was moved by the Yellow Dragon in the River carrying forth a diagram;
upon it were the names of the Eight Trigrams and the myriad phenomena and things. King Wen subsequently doubled them [into the sixty-four hexagrams].
Based on the sixty-four hexagrams, he further composed the *guaci* (hexagram judgments). The Duke of Zhou composed the *yao-ci* (line judgments);
because this system circulated starting from the Zhou dynasty, it is named the *Zhouyi*. As for "Yi," it is formed by combining the two characters for "sun" (*ri*) and "moon" (*yue*).

By placing "moon" beneath "sun" (*rixia cong yue*), it corresponds to the Yin and Yang, taking the meaning of the sun departing and the moon coming; thus it is named "Yi. This was the case during the time of the Zhou.

Originally, it contained only the hexagram texts and the line texts; however, in the final years of his life, Confucius took a great interest in reading them, until the leather bindings were thrice severed.

Thereupon, he composed the commentaries to facilitate their understanding—what are known as the Ten Wings (*Shiyi*). Thus, the Book of Changes (*Zhouyi*) was only fully completed during the time of Confucius.
Consequently, it stands at the beginning of the system of named teachings (*mingjiao*), serves as the foremost of the Six Classics (*liujing*), and is the pinnacle of the Confucian tradition.
Profound mystery reaches its ultimate here; thus it is said that among all the classics, the *Zhouyi* (Changes of Zhou) is the ultimate.

This is why Confucius said, "At fifty, one may study the Changes so as to avoid great error. This is indeed the book for exhausting principle (*li*), perfecting nature (*xing*), and reaching destiny (*ming*).
Destiny is the ultimate limit of life. To exhaust its principle until one reaches destiny is to reach the ultimate perfection. Now, as for the *Yi*:

As this book is both profound and mysterious within the Confucian tradition, and the Confucian school has adopted it as a standard, it is appropriate to cite it to illustrate the principle of ultimate awakening.

[The commentary states: "The virtues of the Buddha—constancy, bliss, selfhood, and purity—are rooted in the one mind. The preceding section cited various categories;

[In order to distinguish this from the deluded attachments of ordinary beings regarding the four inversions: because ordinary beings are deluded, they falsely grasp the impermanent phenomena of the five aggregates and the four great elements as being permanent;

[This is to overturn and refute the four inversions of impermanence and so forth held by the two vehicles. Worldly phenomena are fundamentally not impermanent, fundamentally not suffering, fundamentally not without self, and fundamentally not impure;

[Regarding "the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness" (tathatā-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa): this is the general heading in the treatise. As for "True Suchness" (*tathatā*), speaking from the perspective of the Nature School (*xingzong*):
"True" (*zhen*) means that its essence is free from falsehood and delusion; "Suchness" (*ru*) means that its nature is without change or alteration. Therefore, it is called True Suchness.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called the True Suchness of the Mind is the essence of the single Great Universal Dharma-gate of the One Dharma-realm;

Because its essence is equal toward all ordinary beings and sages, although there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority between the stages of ordinary beings and sages, the self-substance of True Suchness (tathatā) neither increases nor decreases.
From the very beginning, its nature has been spontaneously fulfilled with all merits;

this is the general indication of the characteristic of the Greatness of True Suchness, which possesses all merits. It is not merely the four virtues; this is the general indication of its characteristic of Virtue, namely:

Because its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light, this refers specifically to the characteristic of luminous virtue; that is, the intrinsic awakening-wisdom (mūla-āśraya-jñāna) and its illumination existing within the essence of *tathatā*.

Next, it says: "because it has the meaning of universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu*, because it has the meaning of true and authentic cognition, and because it has the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).
Since these three phrases transcend [the preceding categories], it says "up to and including" (*yāvat*). [Constant Bliss]

Question: What is the purpose of the doctrine of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) here?
Answer: That treatise takes the one mind as its basis; within it, there are two aspects: the mind-as-suchness (*citta-tathatā*) and the mind-as-arising-and-ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha*).
The Gate of the Suchness of the Mind possesses these four virtues. In the Gate of Arising and Ceasing, the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual, and it likewise possesses these four virtues.

Now, while using the four virtues of the Gate of Suchness, we further employ the meaning of the Gate of Arising and Ceasing because the Gate of Suchness is solely the essence (*tattva*), and because within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing, Suchness is also fundamentally based upon the One Mind. Furthermore, as for the essence of the Gate of Suchness...

Because equality is free from all marks, although there are various meanings within the gate of arising and ceasing, their differentiated marks are identical in a single flavor as the one True Suchness.
This is because they are manifested through the marks of arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness;

thus, by means of the marks of the returning consciousness of arising and ceasing, the *saṃsāric* dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges represent the True Suchness, which possesses nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [2. Second, distinguishing from ordinary beings.]

Consciousness is impermanent, yet it is falsely conceptualized as permanent; these four types of false conceptualization are called inversions.

Therefore, in various sūtras, the Buddha causes [practitioners] to cultivate the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of impermanence, and the contemplation of non-self, in order to counteract them.

Below this, the faults of the two vehicles are revealed, refuting the four inversions such as impermanence and so forth, and the conceit of taking non-self to be self.
Ordinary beings falsely conceptualize the five aggregates as a self; therefore, they are made to cultivate the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) in order to shatter their clinging attachments.

Those of the Two Vehicles do not penetrate this principle, yet they rely upon it for their practice, truly asserting that there is no self. This is also a perversion, because they have not realized that within the dharma of non-self there exists the true self;

One constantly perceives the pure as impure and the pleasant as suffering; yet the five aggregates and all phenomena are themselves truly eternal, originally pure, and inherently blissful.
One should understand this according to the above principles. Because they are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), although such conceptions arise, one does not realize their true meaning.
From what do these four inversions (*viparyāsa*) arise? They exist because afflictions shroud that which is truly eternal.

This is because they take the five aggregates to be non-self and thus remain deluded regarding the true self. Therefore, it is termed "birth-and-death. As for "self," it is named...

As for "impermanence," śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are deluded regarding the principle of true permanence; therefore, "permanence" refers to the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. Awakening to impermanent phenomena is itself true permanence.

For the Two Vehicles, the cause is suffering while the fruit is happiness; for Bodhisattvas, both cause and effect are happiness. This "happiness" is precisely Nirvana.

Awakening to the fact that true happiness is inherently present is true Nirvana. That which is impure refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). The preceding discussion regarding correct liberation was not intended to exclude [these categories].
Now, the manifestation of the four virtues of reality (*tattva*) is also included among those to be excluded, because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Regarding the various explanations, we shall now rely on what the Patriarchs commonly cite: (1) the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is that which is capable of universal imagining;

(3) The nature of the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is that which is perfectly accomplished as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness. All...

The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus: according to that school [the Yogācāra], the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is empty because what is falsely conceived by deluded sentiment—such as perceiving a tree stump as a ghost—is not actually a ghost;
therefore, while the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) are definitely existent, emptiness and existence do not coincide.

When the school of the two emptinesses [the Madhyamaka] explains the three natures, it holds that the *paratantra* nature is like a second moon—it has no intrinsic essence from the outset, being dependent from the beginning.
The moon exists, yet it is like a flower in the sky that appears due to a cataract in the dependent eye; to grasp it as truly existent is the parikalpita (imagined nature).

To realize that both the dependent and the imagined are empty is the pariniṣpanna (perfected nature). However, according to that school, the pariniṣpanna is spoken of merely in terms of the principle of the emptiness of the dependent and the imagined;
it lacks any substantial essence. It is like clearing away the clouds across the long expanse of the sky without yet revealing the lunar disc itself.
In the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-vāda*), the three natures are explained as follows: the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like a reflection in a mirror;

the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to such features as the flesh, bones, beauty, or ugliness within that reflection. These two lack intrinsic substance and are merely the perfectly luminous mirror itself, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Thus, it should be understood that the perfected nature taught in the Dharma-nature school is revealed through the very absence of nature in the dependent and imagined natures.
The emergence of the true essence is fundamentally different from those two schools of thought. This means that the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) has no substance;

However, it is precisely because the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* is a pivotal point for all sections of the teachings and elucidates the true single mind that it is classified as the "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*) of the One Vehicle;
thus, its inclusion of both Perfect (*yuan*) and Separate (*bie*) principles is entirely natural. To claim otherwise would be excessive.

Nevertheless, the relative merits of the *Hṛdaya* compared to the *Awakening of Faith* differ significantly, as can be seen by taking the discussion on "breaking and reconciling" (*po hui*) as an illustration. As for that specific discourse:

Some maintain that the final and sudden [teachings] belong to the definitive (real), asserting that this sutra does not belong to the stage of refutation and reconciliation; others maintain that the final and sudden [teachings] are provisional, asserting that this sutra also belongs to the stage of refutation and reconciliation.

However, upon examining this intention, it appears that they are merely debating whether the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuanjue) is identical to or distinct from the provisional, gradual teachings of the first five periods—specifically, whether it is subject to concession or denial, and whether it is included within or excluded from the "refutation and reconciliation" (*po hui*). Since this view contradicts that of Guishan, [it is untenable].
Because it was difficult to receive such an instruction, Qingliang and Bian Guangzhi discussed the conformity and divergence [of their views], saying:

"If one asserts that only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is definitive (*nītārtha*), then this would suppress all the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and other Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning. In the past, there were also both provisional (*neyārtha*) and definitive teachings;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* merely reconciles the former provisional teachings by stating that the three vehicles are all empty. It points to the former reality without being accompanied by expedient means, and therefore does not reconcile them."
(Because it previously explained the principles of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, Nirvāṇa, and the Dharmakāya as truly eternal, this [text] eclipses the Guangzhai [commentary].

If one relies on the past [teachings], it was not yet clearly stated that all beings possess the seeds of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; now, since it is declared that these have been perfected, there is a difference between the past and the present.

(That which was not previously taught is now taught—the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, where the former was provisional and the latter is now the reality—this certainly belongs to the Lotus Sūtra, as is fitting. Now, in the Lotus Sūtra, the śrāvakas of the three capacities are all granted [prediction].)

Because it is recorded, it is said that "now both are explained as established. This then involves conceding [the validity of] Guangzhai’s [system] while refuting various scriptures; this discussion of the conformity or divergence of Guangzhai’s establishment of the teachings results in statements regarding concession and refutation, or the sufficiency and insufficiency of the actual substance, which are formulated as provisional distinctions based on the teachings.

As the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) states: "The explanation has two levels: first, refuting the two vehicles' [view of] real extinction based on phenomena; second, reconciling them based on the teachings, wherein the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna are also integrated. The points of reference differ.
However, according to Qingliang’s intention, regarding the various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other Mahāyāna scriptures prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
That which is called the "Ultimate Teaching" (Zhongjiao) is the sudden exposition of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature within the realm of phenomena; this is called the "Sudden Teaching" (Dunjiao).

Regarding these Ultimate and Sudden teachings, there is both affirmation and negation: they take that substantial reality as insufficient, whether it is categorized as three or one, and whether it is a convergence or a divergence.
How could the single White Ox Cart—the definitive meaning expounded by the Perfect-Sudden (Yuantun) teaching—and its corresponding perfect-capacity recipients, be [limitedly] categorized?

Question: Regarding the three [teachings] being subsumed under one, would it not be a heterodox inquiry? Since the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*) is called "complete" (*yuán*), how does it compare in quality to the *Avataṃsaka*?
Answer: The "Complete" and "Sudden" are discussed in conjunction; there is no distinction between the Sudden and the Complete. As illustrated above, the principles and meanings are clear.

This is evident throughout the commentaries and sub-commentaries. If one were to distinguish them, it would not preclude their having differences, as in the case of what is called "the arising of nature" (*xingqǐ*).

Regarding the "Shared Meaning" (Yìfēn), it is the same as the three contemplations (*sānguān*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; it is also said that this [contemplation] possesses the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).

Furthermore, it is said that this [contemplation] subsumes the Perfect Teaching; however, because this sūtra does not explicitly explain the various Buddha-bodies, lands, sovereignities, unimpeded and vast functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, nor the meanings such as the mutual interpenetration and the layered, harmonious inclusion of all phenomena according to their inherent nature (*dharmatā*), it cannot be called [the Perfect Teaching] in its entirety.
How could the meanings distinguished by the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) ever be confused? Question:

Since the Fundamental Dharma-Wheel (*mūla-dharmacakra*) belongs exclusively to the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda*) also belongs to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), should it likewise be considered a Fundamental Dharma-Wheel?
Answer: The three Dharma-Wheels—Fundamental, Branch, and Final—were established by Jizang. Qingliang remarked that this [classification] is entirely...

If one were to establish [the classification of teachings] based solely on the *huayi* (modes of conversion), this fixed criterion would fail to encompass the full meaning of the Buddha’s lifetime of teaching;

for how could the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* all be considered merely secondary branches? If that were the case, how could they be taken as the sole standard of measurement?
If one insists on using them as the definitive standard, it contradicts the scripture which states: "That which is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods. (Commentary)
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "We, the various Buddhas, protect and uphold this sutra. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "Most of the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras are protected by Śakra-devendra;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is guarded by bodhisattvas; and the *Avataṃsaka* as well as this sutra are protected by the Buddhas themselves.
This is truly because the Root Dharma is the teacher of all Buddhas. Indeed, all that has been recounted above is explicitly stated in the commentaries (*śāstra*) and excerpts.

It is like raising the sun and moon. Having set aside the causes of emotional conceptualization, I immediately offer this verse: "The final three [teachings] become one, opening up both the common and distinct;

ultimately and suddenly they return to the Perfect, which does not meet them in the 'final one. Opening up the common and distinct teachings, the three vehicles of the Initial Teaching belong to provisional expedients;
within the gradual, the Perfect is the ultimate capacity for convergence. The various sutras belong to the five periods, yet the five periods do not pertain [to this ultimate convergence at all]."

Master Cai Zuming of Yuanjue Temple said: "How could one not know that this sutra is distinct from other teachings? It transcends the Separate (Biaojiao) and Common (Tongjiao) schools while sharing the same principle as the Perfect (Yuanjiao).
It is intended for those of perfect capacity and is perfectly sudden. If it were the same as the provisional and gradual, why would Master Guifeng not have frowned in secret?

The *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are called 'shared teachings' (gongjiao), guarded by both Bodhisattvas and devas; the *Yuanjue* and *Avataṃsaka*, however, are the fundamental dharmas of the three periods."
The Tathāgata personally protects and upholds [these teachings, including the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and more than forty other sections].
The *Chan-yuan ch'üan* (Exposition on the Source of Dhyāna) states there are twenty-odd sections; this commentary sometimes says several dozen sections or more than forty sections.

Within these texts, matters and circumstances are seldom discussed, as they directly elucidate the true nature, the principle, and the wisdom. This is because [the teachings] lack such expedient conditions as the three carts, the removal of filth, or the illusory city.

This is because they belong to the same category; thus, one might point to this sutra as being of the same class as the *sudden* (dun) teachings. Question: What distinguishes the various *sudden* sutras from the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué)? Answer:

In terms of revealing the essence (*tǐ*), expounding the Dharma (*fǎ*), and the ritual procedures (*yíshì*), they are all identical. Therefore, none of them belong to the category of "convergence" (*huì*).
However, if within the *sudden* teachings one distinguishes those intended for the capacities of the three vehicles (*sanchéng*), it does not preclude their belonging to the category of convergence.
[The Commentary states: "When the Tathāgata enters the Land of Quiescent Light, ordinary beings and sages share a single source.

Because the essence of the nature of supernatural powers and radiance, as well as its sands-of-the-Ganges virtues and functions, are all contained therein, it is called a "Treasury.

It is also called the Self-Enjoyment Land (*svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*), and it is further stated that this is because the principle and wisdom are undivided. Since this is used to specifically assign [the realm] to the Dharma-nature Land, it employs supernatural powers and great radiance.
The *Samādhi-samāpatti* of the Tiantai school reaches the non-dual state that accords with and pervades the Land of Tranquil Light (*jìguāng tǔ*).

Otherwise, it would not employ the *dharmatā-loka* (Dharma-nature land) of the Characteristics School (*xiàngzōng*). Furthermore, the three lands of the Characteristics School are now employed by our own school; these are simply the three lands of our own school.
It is only that the Patriarchs employed them according to the convenience of the textual meaning, and there is no other doctrine. The four lands of Tiantai are, first, the ordinary world (*fán*).

The four lands are: first, the Land of Mixed Dwelling of Sages; second, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder; third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction; and fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
According to the Abhidharma school (Xiangzong), there are three lands: first, the Land of Transformation; second, the Land of Reward; and third, the Land of Dharma-nature.

If one further distinguishes within the Land of Reward between the lands of self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment, there are likewise four lands. However, Master Tiantai’s four lands were established based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

The Master Yili established the doctrine of the three lands based on the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, stating that since there is clear evidence, this meaning may be relied upon.

Consequently, our school frequently employs the three lands to explain the scriptural texts. However, our school’s freedom in opening or closing [the categories] differs from the School of Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇavāda*);
it also subsumes the first two stages of the Tiantai school. If one opens up the Enjoyment Land into its own and others' aspects, it becomes [four].

The four lands are subsumed within only two types, namely the pure and the defiled; or [the distinction between] the nature-land and the appearance-land. As the *Great Commentary* (Dàshù) states in its later section:

"The three lands and four lands, whether pure or defiled, in terms of nature or appearance, are all inclusively integrated without exception. This is the intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures as well as this present sutra;

thus it is said that they are "fused into one," which differs from other schools. The single land of skillful means (*upāya*) is something not found in the systems of Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

The Abhidharma (Lakṣaṇa) school does not admit that those of the Two Vehicles can turn their minds [toward Mahāyāna]; therefore, it does not establish the existence of a *upāya-bhūmi* (land of skillful means), because according to that school, the Śrāvaka’s departure from the triple world is considered the ultimate goal.
Regarding the phrase "[the body received due to causes and conditions in previous lives]": this refers to the *paricchinna-śarīra* (segmented body).

"One who has departed from the triple world and is free from afflictions" refers to the *nirmāṇa-śarīra* (body of transformation). [Question: Regarding the *upāya-avaśeṣa-bhūmi* (land of skillful means with remainder) mentioned below... [End of excerpt].

Question: It is said that outside the triple world there is a separate Pure Land where those of the Two Vehicles reside; this refers to becoming a Buddha in "other lands" as mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
What kind of body is this "body capable of responding"? Answer: The body capable of responding is precisely the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). As stated in the *Jiaozhang*:
"Some say that Śākyamuni’s reward land is outside the triple world, thirty-two Ganges-sands of worlds to the west."
The "Saha Buddha-land" and the "World Without Superiority" (Anabhibhūta) manifest the transformation land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) of the Buddha of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

this is not his reward body (*vipāka-kāya*). Furthermore, the *Great Commentary on the Profound Meaning* (*Dajie xuantan*) states: "Some say that the reward body exists in other lands; this is spoken of in terms of drawing in and gathering [beings].

Both of these refer to Śākyamuni as either a reward or a transformation body, and both are explained according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*). However, Tiantai, relying on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, [states...]
Citing the *Lotus Sūtra* passage, "I act as a Buddha in other lands," to establish this [present] land, I now likewise cite the explanations of the Patriarchs to respond.

The "Manifest Enjoyment Body" (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) is precisely the "Other Enjoyment Body. The "Self-Enjoyment Body" (*svasaṃbhogika-kāya*) does not admit the vision of those with limited capacities, being identical to the "Dharmatā Body" (*dharmatā-kāya*).
Other than that, the "Other Enjoyment Body" preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings and thus admits such capacities.

Because this is seen, the subsequent text states: "The previous state where ordinary beings and sages share a single source is [the Buddha] entering the Dharma-nature land from his own enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*);
this corresponds to the various bodhisattvas [seeing] him manifest the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) from the Dharma-nature land."
[The "Explanatory Commentary on the Initial Arising"] refers to the very first mind that arises from causes.

To suddenly awaken to the originally existing, wondrously enlightened mind (*bodhicitta*), which is fundamentally free from ignorance and birth-and-death, is what is called true and correct faith-and-understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*).
To unite this true and correct faith-and-understanding with the Tathāgata’s initial cause—that is, the fundamental mind originally arisen by the Buddha—is to realize this wondrously enlightened mind.
Since this serves as the fundamental basis for all Tathāgatas, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one does not understand the mind—that is, one's own mind—how can one know the true path?
Even if one practices for many kalpas, one is not a true Bodhisattva. [This involves awakening to the two types of enlightenment, giving rise to the three minds, and practicing the five virtues.
Now, in the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) according to the Sudden Teaching, there are generally three levels; the first is initial realization and understanding.
After awakening to the nature of mind (*buddhatā*), one next arouses the bodhicitta and then cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva.

In the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Dasheng qixin lun*) as well, it first reveals the two types of awakening, then instructs one to arouse the three minds, and only thereafter does one cultivate the five practices. The "two awakenings" refer to the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).

The "three minds" refer to the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), and the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*). The "cultivation of the five practices" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) combined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Question: Since wisdom is singular, does the arising of faith belong exclusively to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), and how could it possess all three levels of causes?

Answer: The gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*) also possesses the meaning of the Sudden Teaching and is intended for those with sudden capacities. The *Dachao* states: "It also penetrates both sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.

Master Xuanshou judged it to be the primary Final Teaching while simultaneously encompassing the Sudden; Guishan’s commentary on the treatise is likewise so. Therefore, the treatise says: "The arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith."

There are three kinds, namely the upright mind (*ṛju-citta*), the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), and the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*) listed above. The *Xiuzheng yi* (Ritual for Cultivation and Realization) states:

"Since the gate of faith in the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) subsumes [all stages] instantaneously, one should know that what is taught in that treatise regarding the ground of causes (*hetu-bhūmi*) possesses these three aspects, as detailed below in section eight.

Furthermore, in the *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra), the *Śāriputra-parivarta*, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-dharmacaryā*, Sudhana first declares what he has already accomplished before asking his questions.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra on the Gate of Practice* states: "If a bhikṣu recites the twelve divisions of the scriptures, expounds them for the assembly, and contemplates their meaning, he is not called one who practices the Dharma (*dharmacārin*).

If a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the spheres of body and mind such that they are entirely stilled and he is forever detached from afflictions, with his mind in tranquility, I then declare him to be one who practices the Dharma. [The Bhagavat] is also named...
The *Bhagavad-vyākhyā* states: "One who can destroy the afflictions is named Bhagavat. This corresponds to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), by which the Dharmakāya is manifested.

Regarding the teaching of the Pure Land through the exposition of the Dharma, the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (*sambhogakāya*) are not distinguished; this refers to the [Dharmakāya], not the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Although these six meanings—namely, the first two being the virtue of abandonment within the Dharmakāya, the middle two being the virtue of wisdom within the Sambhogakāya, and the final two being the virtue of grace within the Nirmāṇakāya—pervade all three bodies, they are nonetheless associated with each specifically.
Regarding the different ways in which "virtue" (*guṇa*) appears across various sutras: in this sutra, it corresponds to the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

in the provisional and gradual sutras, it corresponds to the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*) of the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This does not preclude other sutras from also [possessing these virtues]. The *Bāghabāda Daichao* states:

"In the Perfect and Sudden teachings of the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, there is the True Body in which principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) are inseparable; this sutra is the teaching of the Pure Land."

Therefore, the Lord of Transformation is the True Body (dharmakāya). Thus, the *Bhagavat-buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that this is the manifestation of the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) as the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Consequently, there is a distinction in how those on the stages (*bhūmi*) and those below the stages perceive it.

This sūtra concerns the True Body in which the Dharma-body and Reward-body are undivided; its meaning of mutual identity differs from that [of the aforementioned sūtra]. However, among the three meanings presented in the Commentary...

The *Nyāya* (Righteousness) is the primary exponent of this sutra, while the *Saṃdhinirmocana* (Unraveling the Intent) is the primary exponent of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*) sutra, because that [latter] sutra communicates both the Truth-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the "six meanings," these are alternative translations; if translated directly, it is "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come-One), and the direct translation is "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavat*).
Furthermore, this commentary states: "It means that all Tathāgatas are not bound by any afflictions (*kleśa*). From this, one may know [the meaning].

"Gold has no heavy ore" means that while the principle is realized all at once (*tunwu*), the afflictive obstructions (*nīvaraṇa*) are removed gradually. Thus, the subsequent scripture states:

[The Principle is Beyond Cultivation and Realization] The nature of awakening is equal, originally devoid of the distinction between the holy and the ordinary;

how could there be cultivation or realization? Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The nature is inherently equal, yet there is no 'equality' [to be attained]. This is because it is spoken of as "sentient beings" in reference to the presence of defilements, and as "bodhisattvas" in contrast to the removal of illusory defilements.
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*), there are in fact no manifold characteristics. Thus, one knows this to be Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

The fundamental nature is utterly beyond cultivation and realization. Regarding the phrase "non-nature yet nature exists," the Commentary states that "non-nature" refers to the five preceding natures and the differentiated natures of saṃsāra.
"Nature exists" means that these differentiated natures all possess the Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti’s *Awakening of Faith*);

it is like the vajra-dharmakāya, which is not the marks of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), yet the marks of excellence are not separate from the dharmakāya. This is illustrated by the analogy of gold: the gold is not the lion, yet there is gold within the lion.
"Cultivation" means "following. This refers to the fact that this awakened nature does not abide in its own nature, but follows along with various differentiated natures as they arise.
When these differentiated natures arise, the gold-like awakened nature arises; yet the awakened nature remains equal and without grasping or realization, just as the eye cannot see itself.

Awakening is called the stage of the worthy; the three stages of the sages are those capable of awakening to the aforementioned obstacles to understanding and obstacles to awakening.

Since both these obstacles are themselves obstructive, the illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescent extinction. This is like wisdom being equal and devoid of the characteristics of subject and object. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"When obstacles have already been severed and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes the obstacles; this is called the stage of the sages. As for the four fruits of the path, they are the aforementioned... [various stages].

they are fundamentally one's own mind, inherently self-aware and self-knowing. There is no need to give rise to further cognition upon what is already known.

Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not the liberation of the ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm; its illumination and realization of all phenomena as being like space is termed the "fruition stage.

The present commentary states that "causes and conditions" here refers to the aforementioned general meaning, without distinguishing between proximity and remoteness. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, being a teaching that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), was taught at the very beginning; therefore, its manifestation was originally for the sake of the Great *Avataṃsaka*.

The Victorious One does not give rise to thought for even a single moment; with the continuity of past and future severed, he attains Buddhahood through sudden awakening to non-thought.

If one can understand this state, and if one’s contemplative practice is perfected such that one understands this state, it is identical to attaining Buddhahood at the completion of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The principles and meanings addressed in this sutra are not distinct from those previously asked; as for those who find them difficult to understand, Vajragarbha is one capable of both raising such doubts and resolving them—one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*).
If doubt is eliminated upon the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) through discernment, how could a practitioner who has ascended the stages harbor such doubts?
Furthermore, since the Buddha examined Vajragarbha’s questions and found them appropriate, it must be that Vajragarbha truly possessed these [doubts].
Regarding the question of doubt, the *Bǎifǎchāo* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas) states: Vajragarbha of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "Because of this, doubt arises and one follows the evil paths.

The *Daichao* (Great Commentary) contains the phrase "the mind capable of faith" following "the teachings heard," and its clarification of errors states: "Hearing permeates faith."

Now, when one is required to make a selection, if the object of faith is absent—having discarded the various permeations of what has been heard—then the mind capable of faith will naturally be absent as well. Thus says the *Dàchǎo*.
This current abridgment includes [the necessary elements]; though concise, its meaning is not deficient. Based on these conditions and seeds, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:

"Faith is difficult to understand. [If there are seeds regarding the Dharma, it is easy to understand. The *Dàochào* states that this also applies to what is "easy to believe," yet the present *Chāo* omits this because understanding necessarily entails faith.

if there is no power of aspiration and commitment, then one cannot achieve the mutual guidance of compassion and wisdom to realize the dwelling in non-abiding. Because of great compassion, one does not abide in nirvana;
because of great wisdom, one does not abide in saṃsāra. By departing from these two extremes, the Middle Way is realized—all of this is due to the power of the great vow.

It is so called because the Buddhas have attained it, because it is beyond the capacities of sentient beings, and because it transcends verbal teaching; thus, it is the ocean of the perfection of inherent nature.
The Worthy One (Bhadramukha) maintains that the fruition-aspect of the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra-phala-bhāga*) is an ineffable meaning.

Regarding the possession of the two aforementioned meanings, first we clarify the unification of the three vehicles into one: this involves taking up the former three and subsequently clarifying the unification of those former three into the single vehicle of the present, thereby abolishing the former three to establish the single vehicle of the present. If we consider this in terms of "taking up" (*yǒu*), then even the former Small Vehicle is taken up, because its practice constitutes the cause for Buddhahood.

If we consider this in terms of "abolishing" (*fèi*), then even the former Great Vehicle is abolished, because its teachings are established as provisional and its fruits are likewise pointed out as provisional. Thus, regarding the teaching (*jiào*), the three are abolished and the one is established; regarding the principle (*lǐ*), the three are opened to reveal the one; regarding practice (*xíng*), the three are subsumed into the one;

and regarding the fruit (*guǒ*), the three are unified and returned to the one. These three aspects—opening, subsuming, and unifying—mutually interpenetrate, each encompassing these three meanings. However, the principles of abolition and establishment apply only to the teaching and do not extend to the other three aspects. The three dots (*diǎn*) serve as a metaphor for the Three Vehicles, which together form the character *ī* (*yī*) to symbolize the One Vehicle.

Regarding the vehicles, they are separately taught as three, yet all three are provisional; by uniting the three into one, they may be called the true Dharma. Now, this one [vehicle] fully encompasses them; thus, combining the former "I" (the horizontal stroke) with the three points to form four is without error.
